transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
The Pentagon has acknowledged U.S. casualties in the war with Iran are higher than previously announced.
As NPR's Quill Lawrence reports, 22 Americans have died since the war began.
A Pentagon spokesman told NPR the way casualties are being counted is being standardized
and that the department will begin posting numbers that are "pending adjudication" and may change.
But this is not the first time the Trump administration has abruptly posted new numbers
or changed the way it counts casualties from the Iran war, spreading the numbers of wounded in action,
killed in action, and non-combat casualties as if they were not part of the same war.
Two leading Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee said in a statement that while they were glad to see the error had been corrected,
there is "no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude."
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
Cleanup is underway after Hurricane Isaias, now a post-tropical cyclone, left at least four people dead
and hundreds of thousands of customers without power.
NPR's Debbie Elliott reports the storm made landfall last night near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane.
Hurricane Isaias came ashore with 105-mile-an-hour winds, a five-foot storm surge, and heavy rainfall,
causing damage from the Alabama Gulf Coast into the Florida Panhandle.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis says emergency crews are working now to clear down trees and power lines and repair damaged water systems.
It's still a very hazardous situation. All the assets are there to get the power back on, make sure all the roads are clean and safe.
And that's being done. But just please continue to exercise caution in the next couple of days.
The remnants of Isaias are moving across the southeast with a risk of flash flooding. Debbie Elliott, NPR News, Crestview, Florida.
A growing number of voters are using AI chatbots to research their ballot and help them decide between candidates for the upcoming midterms.
As NPR's Maham Devade reports, the trend cuts across party lines.
One in five U.S. voters say they consult AI chatbots for election news and voting.
And the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation says Democratic and Republican voters are using AI chatbots at similar rates.
There are concerns that the bots can be subtly persuasive and perhaps agreeable to a fault.
Adam Johnson is a voter in West Virginia who has used chat GPT to research his ballot.
Chat GPT is just kind of a people pleaser. It just aims to please.
So whatever you lean towards, it will speak positively about it.
Experts say these attributes can leave readers feeling more confident about their knowledge.
You're listening to NPR News.
The public comment period closed this week for a federal proposal to gut the standards for the nation's largest early education program.
Tens of thousands of people posted their concerns.
NPR's Sequoia Carrillo reports.
The Trump administration's proposed changes to the Head Start program garnered more than 40,000 comments over the last two months.
The administration says the move to take 133 pages of guidelines and reduce it to only a handful is meant to reduce administrative burden on Head Start centers.
But advocates say the move will undermine the program's standard of care.
The six-year-old anti-poverty program provides preschool and childcare along with meals and support services for qualifying families.
The program serves more than 700,000 kids each year from birth to age five.
The proposal now goes back to the Trump administration to reply to public comment.
Sequoia Carrillo, NPR News.
Mortgage rates have ticked higher for the seventh week in a row, driving the average long-term home loan rate to its highest level in nearly three years.
Mortgage buyer Freddie Mac reports the 30-year fixed rate mortgage climbed to 7.40 percent from 7.28 percent last week.
One year ago, the average rate was 6.30 percent.
The average rate is now the highest since November 16th of 2023, when it was at 7.44 percent.
Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs to borrowers.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
